source_text: Ad quod tamen quasi corollarium peculiaris sceleris adiunxit, ut talem poenam a Deo illatam diceret, quae esset illecebra et fomes peccati, quae lex in membris invicta repugnaret legi mentis nostrae; quo genere ultionis multiplicaret Deus flagitia, non puniret; et qui iratus erat malae voluntati, qua fuerat erratum, reliquum faceret peccandi necessitatem. Quale sit tamen hoc iudicium, Manichaei furor viderit; dum constet, quia hic iudex qui ab Augustino fingitur, simularit se horrere peccatum, caeterum tanto eis adhaeret affectu, ut diligentiorem nutritium invenire non possint.
pass_a_gloss: To which nevertheless he joined as a kind of corollary of peculiar wickedness, that he would say such a penalty was inflicted by God as would be a lure and tinder of sin, as a law in the members unconquered would fight against the law of our mind; by which kind of vengeance God would multiply outrages, not punish them; and he who was angry at the evil will by which it had been erred, would make the rest a necessity of sinning. Of what sort this judgment is, nevertheless, the fury of Manichaeus may see; while it stands that this judge who is feigned by Augustine pretended to shudder at sin, but for the rest clings to them with so great affection that they cannot find a more diligent nurse.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: As though to crown this with a wickedness all his own, he added that God inflicted a punishment that was a lure and fuel for sin: a law in our members fighting unconquered against the law of our mind (compare Romans 7:23). By this sort of vengeance God would multiply crimes, not punish them. Having been angry at the evil will by which the sin was committed, he would make sinning a necessity thereafter. Let Manichaean frenzy decide what kind of judgment this is. At least it is clear that this judge invented by Augustine only pretends to abhor sin. In reality, he clings to sins with such affection that they could not find a more attentive nurse (Romans 7:23).

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
